entries.title: Van Hollen Says Senators Aren’t Publicly Supporting Him Due to Fear of Schumer ‘Retaliation’
entries.summary: A number of Senate Democrats said Monday they were waiting to have a debate with the rest of the caucus before announcing their pick for majority leader.
entries.content:
Most Democratic senators are publicly staying neutral on the race for majority leader between Chuck Schumer and his challenger, Sen. Chris Van Hollen.

Only four members of the Democratic caucus have publicly stated their support for Van Hollen so far: Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), Jeff Merkley (D-Oregon), and Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Michigan) and Peggy Flanagan (D-Minnesota), with many more demurring on Monday night. But Van Hollen thinks he has more support from his colleagues than is known and attributes their silence to a fear of angering Schumer.

“What you've got obviously is somebody who has the power of incumbency and so there is an element of concern about political retaliation,” the Maryland Democrat told The Washington Sun. “So it's hard to ask people to be public when they're worried that it will lead to bad consequences.”

Around 15 senators are supporting Schumer — still short of the close to 30 votes required to be reelected Democratic leader.

Van Hollen disputed reports that Schumer had already locked up the race to become leader.

“There was some article that came out that listed a bunch of people as having committed to Schumer, where I know for a fact some have said they're voting for me, and others I know are undecided on that list,” Van Hollen said Monday, insisting that he has a path.

The 67-year-old progressive senator has pitched himself as a change candidate who backs more aggressive tactics to end the Iran war and cut off U.S. aid to Israel. He’s also been critical of Schumer for wading into contested Democratic primary fights this year and for his stance opposing President Barack Obama’s nuclear deal with Iran.

Many of his colleagues say they’d welcome a discussion about leadership changes but credit Schumer with flipping as many as nine Senate seats in the midterm elections.

“We just had the single greatest results in a midterm election in a generation, and Leader Schumer was central to a lot of the recruitment and fundraising,” Sen. Chris Coons (D-Delaware) told The Sun. He described Van Hollen’s chances of becoming leader as “remote.”

Even Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, the junior senator from Maryland, declined to take a position on Van Hollen’s leadership bid.

“We’re going to have a big, big discussion tomorrow. We'll figure it out,” Alsobrooks said.

Sen. Mazie Hirono of Hawaii was the only Democrat who made news in announcing her support for leader as senators returned to Washington for a pair of votes on Monday.

“I have a long history with Chuck. He's helped me on some pretty necessary things that are really important to Hawaii,” Hirono told reporters.

Others, like Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Virginia), laid out the case for both sides.

“No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer. Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in Congress,” Kaine said, though he added that “the voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change.”



Democratic senators also poured cold water on the idea of moving up the vote instead of holding it on Dec. 1, as originally scheduled, to help Schumer. Allies of the Democratic leader were reportedly pushing to hold an earlier vote.

“I haven’t heard that seriously proposed,” Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Georgia) said. “But I would oppose expediting before we've had a full process.”

And since the vote will take place via secret ballot, the public may never know how some senators voted.

“I am not telling one way or the other,” said Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey), who’s considering a 2028 presidential bid. “It's a secret ballot.”

entries.title: Ecuadorian Fishermen Injured in Drone Attack Sue the Trump Administration
entries.summary: The crew said the March attack sank their fishing boat and severely burned two men. They’re asking a federal judge to halt lethal U.S. boat strikes in the Pacific and Caribbean.
entries.content:
A crew of Ecuadorian fishermen sued the Trump administration Monday, alleging that drones launched from an American vessel sank their fishing boat in the Pacific Ocean and left two crew members with severe burns.

The lawsuit filed in the Western District of Pennsylvania seeks damages and an order ending lethal U.S. boat strikes in the Pacific and Caribbean. It gives grisly, firsthand details of the crew of La Negra Francesca Duarte II, who say the United States tortured and mocked them after misidentifying them as narcotics traffickers.

“Jordy’s leg was burned to the bone, and he bled profusely,” the complaint says of crew member Jordy Flores Lucas. “As a result of this attack, La Negra Francesca Duarte II was totally engulfed with flames and destroyed. The U.S. then kidnapped the surviving fishermen and held them against their will for around 24 hours.”

The Trump administration has claimed responsibility for carrying out missile and drone strikes — attacks the military argues target "narco-terrorists" in the Pacific — but has declined knowledge and responsibility for the attack on La Negra Francesca Duarte II and other Ecuadorean vessels destroyed earlier this year.

The fishermen say the Ecuadorian navy cleared their boat after a three-hour inspection shortly before the March 17 attack.

Following the bombardment, the crew escaped in small boats and approached a nearby ship, where armed personnel gave Flores Lucas medical care and zip-tied and hooded the others, according to the suit. The fishermen allege they were then “forced to stand barefoot on the iron deck which was very hot” and later taken to El Salvador where they were held against their will.

Flores Lucas recalled that military personnel showed him a drawing of the attack and “laughed about what they had done and about how they had destroyed the fishing vessel.”

The lawsuit alleges their treatment in U.S. custody amounted to torture, adding that the government has carried out the strikes without congressional authorization.

Last December, Democratic Reps. Jamie Raskin and Ted Lieu asked the Justice Department to investigate whether a separate Caribbean strike that killed survivors clinging to wreckage amounted to a war crime or murder.
